documents.title: Guidelines for the management of acute cervical spine and spinal cord injuries

chunks.content: Introduction Chronic high‐level spinal cord injury (SCI) is characterized by a complex cardiovascular phenotype. The disruption of efferent medullary sympathetic signalling to the spinal cord results in profound haemodynamic instability, long‐term blood pressure dysregulation and increased risk of cardiovascular disease (Cragg et al., ; Furlan et al., ; Krassioukov & Claydon, ; Teasell et al., ). While the heart is central to these outcomes, our understanding of the acute and chronic cardiac consequences of SCI has only recently begun to unfold. In a recent series of studies, our group utilized direct left ventricular (LV) catheterization to demonstrate an immediate impairment to cardiac contractility following high‐level SCI (Williams et al., ). This decline of intrinsic cardiac function persists chronically and is linked to a loss of bulbospinal sympathetic control (Ahmadian et al., ; Fossey et al., ). From a clinical perspective, neuroprotection is paramount in the early stages of an acute traumatic SCI. The loss of sympathetic tone and resultant ‘neurogenic shock’ that accompanies high‐level traumatic SCI (i.e. injuries at or above the T6 segment) pose a threat to neurological recovery; as such, hypotension can further limit spinal cord perfusion and exacerbate secondary damage (Ahuja et al., ; Tator & Fehlings, ). Vasopressor‐based haemodynamic management is currently recommended to offset these pressure challenges (Kwon et al., ); however, achieving and maintaining a standardized target mean arterial pressure (MAP) is challenging in practice (Gee et al., ) and vasopressor management can risk worsening haemorrhage at the site of injury (Cheung et al., ; Guha et al., ; Soubeyrand et al., ). Importantly, while conventional focus has primarily surrounded the peripheral vasculature, the role of the heart has received less clinical attention in the acute phase of SCI. Acknowledging these research gaps, we recently explored a cardio‐centric approach to haemodynamic management using the cardiac β‐agonist dobutamine (DOB) to restore LV contractility in the acute phase following experimental T2 SCI in pigs (Williams et al., ). DOB administration not only elevated MAP over the course of treatment, but also enhanced spinal cord oxygenation and mitigated the extent of spinal cord haemorrhage that occurred with vasopressor treatment (i.e. norepinephrine, NE). It remains to be determined whether such a cardio‐centric approach is associated with improved long‐term cardiovascular and neurological outcomes following high‐level SCI. Accordingly, the current research aimed to characterize the potential long‐term benefits of acute cardio‐centric management. We utilized our porcine model of T2 SCI to examine chronic cardiovascular and neurological outcomes associated with acute DOB‐ versus NE‐based haemodynamic management. By combining invasive LV pressure–volume (PV), right‐heart and arterial pressure catheterization, we characterized resting and dynamic cardiovascular function (i.e. contractile reserve and baroreflex responses) in animals that survived for 12 weeks post‐SCI, and additionally conducted validated neurological assessments on a weekly basis in these animals. Methods Ethics Ethical approval was obtained from the University of British Columbia Animal Care Committee (A16‐0311) and United States Department of Defense (IACUC #A16‐0311). All procedures were compliant with the Canadian Council on Animal Care policies. The investigators understand the ethical principles under which the journal operates and that their work complies with the animal ethics checklist as outlined by the journal. Prior publications of data Preliminary analyses of outcome data have been previously reported for a subset of the animals in the current study (Williams et al., ). Specifically, data from n = 10 animals ( n = 4 for DOB, n = 3 for NE and CON) were presented for assessments of resting end‐systolic elastance (E es ), MAP, total peripheral resistance (TPR) and arterial elastance (E a ) at 12 weeks post‐SCI. The remainder of the data are unique to this manuscript. Animal care A total of 20 female Yucatan minipigs (age 4–6 months at the start of experiments, 22–32 kg; S&S Farms, Ramona, CA, USA) were acquired and housed in the Centre for Comparative Medicine facility at the University of British Columbia. Animals were housed for 1–2 weeks prior to SCI surgery in pairs of groups of 3–4 animals, in indoor pens with sawdust bedding and access to an adjoining outdoor pen. Animals were provided with enrichment (e.g. toys such as chains and balls), feed equal to 1.5% of body mass twice per day, and water ad libitum . Animals were habituated to humans with daily visits from researchers prior to surgery. From 0 up to 14 days after SCI, pain management was achieved via fentanyl administration (0.45–6.5 µg/kg/h) via continuous rate infusion (CRI) only, via CRI and transdermal patch, or via transdermal patch only, depending on the stage of recovery and process of analgesia wean‐off. When animals were receiving CRI fentanyl, they were monitored 24/7 so pump failures or flow occlusions could be rectified immediately, and the continuous delivery of analgesic ensured. From 0 up to 14 days after SCI, pain management was achieved via fentanyl administration (0.45–6.5 µg/kg/h) via continuous rate infusion (CRI) only, via CRI and transdermal patch, or via transdermal patch only, depending on the stage of recovery and process of analgesia wean‐off. When animals were receiving CRI fentanyl, they were monitored 24/7 so pump failures or flow occlusions could be rectified immediately, and the continuous delivery of analgesic ensured. Animals were transitioned from CRI fentanyl to transdermal fentanyl to prepare for their transition from an enclosed clamshell to a modified open floor pen. In general, the fentanyl transdermal patches were placed on the axilla of forelimbs and was supplemented with another patch 12 h prior to the initial patch expiring (patches are efficacious for 72 h), but replacement frequency could be adjusted on an as need basis, determined by the facility veterinarian. Assessments of pain, using the porcine grimace scoring scale, was carried out at least five times per day between 07.00 h and 23.00 h and the dosage of fentanyl adjusted to maintain adequate pain control. The clinical veterinarians in consultation with the research team and research veterinary technicians made decisions regarding pain control. The fentanyl dose was gradually reduced until stopped as signs of pain diminished and subsided. All research veterinarians and technicians were blinded to the animal's treatment group. Once sufficiently recovered, animals were returned to their pens and again housed in pairs with additional enrichment. The pens had sawdust bedding and padded walls, and plastic mats were additionally placed to mitigate slipping and scrapes. Over the 12‐week recovery period, research staff checked on animals multiple times per day and night, helping to reposition animals if they became stuck or tipped on their sides. Ambulation, body temperature, heart rate (HR), pressure ulcers, bowel and bladder function were monitored daily, and urinary catheters were removed if, and when, animals regained their ability to void the bladder. Surgical preparation and anaesthesia for SCI surgery Animals were fasted for 12 h prior to SCI surgery, and pre‐anaesthetized intramuscular injections telazol (4–6 mg kg −1 ), xylazine (1 mg kg −1 ) and atropine (0.02–0.04 mg kg −1 ). On the morning of the surgery, animals were induced with propofol (2 mg kg −1 ), then endotracheally intubated for mechanical ventilation (10–12 breaths min −1 ; tidal volume 12–15 mg kg −1 ; Veterinary Anesthesia Ventilator model 2002, Hallowell EMC, Pittsfield, MA). A urinary catheter was placed for intra‐operative bladder drainage (10 F, Jorgensen Laboratories Inc., Loveland, CO), and intravenous catheters for administration of anaesthetic agents and fluids. A rectal temperature probe was placed to monitor core body temperature, which was maintained at 38.5–39.5°C using a heating pad (T/Pump, Gaymar Industries, Inc., Orchard Park, NY). Intravenous CRIs of propofol (6–12 mg kg −1 h −1 ), fentanyl (6–14 mg kg −1 h −1 ) and ketamine (4–14 mg kg −1 h −1 ) were provided for anaesthesia during the surgery, and intravenous fluids were given to maintain hydration (7–10 ml kg −1 h −1 , 2.5% dextrose + 0.9% NaCl). The surgical plane of anaesthesia was determined by the absence of jaw tone, as assessed by veterinary technicians. Standard monitoring was performed for HR (electrocardiogram), respiratory rate, end‐tidal carbon dioxide and oxygen saturation (pulse oximeter 8600 V, Nonin Medical Inc., Markham, ON). Blood pressure was monitored via tail or ear catheterization, with the aim of avoiding any potential damage to the hindlimbs that could have affected motor recovery over the course of the study. Cardiopulmonary instrumentation prior to SCI Following induction, animals were transferred to an operating table and placed in a supine orientation. With the support of a cardiac surgeon (K.T.) we developed a methodology to percutaneously place a Swan‐Ganz pulmonary artery catheter. The intent of this approach was to mitigate the haemodynamic risks and potential tissue damage associated with direct access (i.e. cutting down to the jugular vein), while simultaneously allowing for repeated measures of cardiac output (via thermodilution) and pulmonary pressures throughout the experimental protocol, notably during the haemodynamic management period. The Swan‐Ganz catheters were first placed into a jugular vein using ultrasound guidance, then advanced to the pulmonary artery under fluoroscopic guidance. Placement in the pulmonary artery was confirmed via visualization of the pulmonary artery pressure waveform. T2 contusion SCI Following catheterization, animals were shifted into a prone position on the operating table. A laminectomy was first performed to expose the spinal cord from the C8–T4 level, then a weight‐drop impactor device with a guide rail and articulating arm (660, Starrett, Athol, MA) was mounted onto a metal base and attached with pedicle screws to the T1 and T4. The impactor tip (0.953 cm diameter) was vertically oriented above

Placement in the pulmonary artery was confirmed via visualization of the pulmonary artery pressure waveform. T2 contusion SCI Following catheterization, animals were shifted into a prone position on the operating table. A laminectomy was first performed to expose the spinal cord from the C8–T4 level, then a weight‐drop impactor device with a guide rail and articulating arm (660, Starrett, Athol, MA) was mounted onto a metal base and attached with pedicle screws to the T1 and T4. The impactor tip (0.953 cm diameter) was vertically oriented above the exposed cord at the T2 level. The impactor device included a load cell in the impactor tip (LLB215, Futek Advanced Sensor Technology, Irvine, CA) and a linear position sensor in the guide rail (Balluff Micropulse, Balluff Canada Inc., Mississauga, ON) to quantify the impactor force and position during the weight drop and SCI. LabVIEW software (v16.0, National Instruments, Austin, TX) was used to remotely operate the impactor and simultaneously monitor the force and position data in real time. Animals received a CRI of fentanyl (7 µg kg −1 over 1 min) 5 min prior to the SCI, at which point a 50 g cylinder plastic weight was dropped through the guide rail from a height of approximately 20 cm. An additional 100 g weight was immediately added for a total 150 g compression. At 2 h post‐SCI the 150 g of weight was removed for decompression, after which the pedicle screws were removed and the screw holes in the vertebral body were closed with bone wax. Haemodynamic management and cardiopulmonary data We initially sought to ensure that it was feasible for the animal to survive for a full 12 weeks with this severe and high‐level of SCI. Thus, from a total of 20 animals, the initial two animals were assigned as controls (CON) and did not receive haemodynamic management. Once those animals were successfully recovered over 12 weeks, an additional 18 animals were randomized and counterbalanced to receive haemodynamic management with continuous infusions of DOB (2.5 µg kg −1 min −1 , n = 7), NE (4.25 µg kg −1 min −1 , n = 8) or no treatment (CON, n = 5 total). These specific dosages were determined as the mean effective doses from the DOB and NE animals from our prior acute study (Williams et al., ), wherein infusions of NE were adjusted to attain a target MAP of 85–90 mmHg, and DOB was adjusted to attain an E es of ∼2.5–2.9 mmHg ml −1 . Haemodynamic management began at 30 min post‐SCI and continued until 6 h post‐SCI, at which point the Swan‐Ganz catheter was removed and animals were recovered for 12 weeks post‐SCI (Fig. ). During the SCI experiments, pulmonary pressures (i.e. pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP) and mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP)) were continuously monitored via the Swan‐Ganz catheter from baseline (pre‐SCI) until 6 h post‐SCI, and thermodilution assessments of cardiac output (Q TD ) were performed at baseline, 30 min (just prior to management) and hourly up to 6 h post‐SCI. During the recovery period, three animals did not survive: two NE‐treated animals and one DOB‐treated animal were killed humanely prior to the 12 week end‐point. Therefore, data from a total of 17 animals were included in the final analyses: n = 5 for CON, n = 6 for DOB and n = 6 for NE. Transthoracic echocardiography Echocardiographic imaging was performed following induction and intubation, prior to all cardiopulmonary instrumentation. Animals were positioned supine and rotated slightly to the left to optimize imaging windows. All images were acquired by a highly trained research sonographer (A.M.W.) using a commercially available ultrasound (Vivid i, GE Healthcare) and 1.5–3.6 MHz transducer (M4S probe, GE Healthcare, Fairfield CT). LV parasternal long‐axis images were recorded over 10 consecutive cardiac cycles, and analysed offline for LV internal diameter at end‐diastole (LVID d ). Measurements were taken during the expiratory period and averaged over three cardiac cycles. These echocardiographic assessments were repeated at 12 weeks post‐SCI. End‐point surgery and anaesthesia at 12 weeks post‐SCI Animals were induced and transferred into a supine position on an operating table for cardiovascular instrumentation. The protocol for anaesthesia was identical to that during the SCI surgery, and drug levels were maintained as closely as possible to those administered during the SCI experiments. For cardiac catheterization, a 5 cm incision was made in the tissue above the right jugular vein, and the carotid artery and external jugular vein were revealed with blunt dissection. A pig‐tailed admittance PV catheter (5F; Sciscence Catheter and ADVantage PV System (ADV500), Transonic Systems Inc.) and a Swan‐Ganz catheter (7.5 F; Edwards Lifesciences Canada Inc., Mississauga, ON) were connected to an A/D board (PowerLab, ADInstruments, Colorado Springs, MO) and data

instrumentation. The protocol for anaesthesia was identical to that during the SCI surgery, and drug levels were maintained as closely as possible to those administered during the SCI experiments. For cardiac catheterization, a 5 cm incision was made in the tissue above the right jugular vein, and the carotid artery and external jugular vein were revealed with blunt dissection. A pig‐tailed admittance PV catheter (5F; Sciscence Catheter and ADVantage PV System (ADV500), Transonic Systems Inc.) and a Swan‐Ganz catheter (7.5 F; Edwards Lifesciences Canada Inc., Mississauga, ON) were connected to an A/D board (PowerLab, ADInstruments, Colorado Springs, MO) and data were collected and visualized in real time using commercially available software (LabChart PRO v8.1.9, ADInstruments). The PV catheter was inserted with an introducer (12F; Fast‐Cath Hemostasis Introducer, Abbott) and advanced until an arterial waveform was visualized, and the Swan‐Ganz catheter was placed in the external jugular vein and advanced until a right ventricular waveform was visualized. Thereafter, both catheters were advanced under fluoroscopic guidance (Arcadis Avantic, Siemens Healthcare Limited, Oakville, ON) to ensure accurate placement of the PV catheter in the LV and the Swan‐Ganz catheter in the pulmonary artery. Animals were additionally instrumented with bilateral femoral arterial catheters as described previously (Williams et al., ) with fluid‐filled lines connected to the A/D board to monitor blood pressure (MAP, systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP)). Sutures were placed to secure the catheters in their respective vessels and close the dissected tissue. End‐point assessments of cardiopulmonary function Once stable levels of anaesthesia and haemodynamics (i.e. MAP, HR) were attained, ‘baseline’ or resting data collection began. Transient inferior vena cava (IVC) occlusions were performed over 10–15 cardiac cycles for offline calculations of load‐independent LV function, including end‐systolic elastance (E es ), preload‐recruitable stroke work (PRSW) and LV end‐diastolic pressure‐volume relationship (EDPVR). Following baseline, LV contractile reserve was assessed using a DOB stress test, specifically involving a constant‐rate infusion of DOB (10 µg kg −1 min −1 ) for 10 min with transient IVC occlusions performed in the final 3 min. Following at least 30 min recovery (≥5 DOB half‐life (Ruffolo, )), a modified Oxford challenge (0.1 mg sodium nitroprusside (SNP) bolus followed by 0.1 mg phenylephrine (PE) bolus 45 s after) was performed to assess the cardiac responses to blood pressure challenges. Once data collection was complete, animals were killed by i.v. injection of sodium pentobarbital (120 mg/kg), prior to tissue harvesting. In the cases where killing was required because an animal reached the humane end‐point, they were first pre‐medicated with subcutaneous telazol (5 mg/kg) and xylazine (1 mg/kg), then sedated with inhaled isoflurane (to effect) in order to place an i.v. catheter for the delivery of sodium pentobarbital (120 mg/kg). In both instances, death was ascertained by the cessation of respiration and an absence of a heartbeat. Analyses of cardiopulmonary data Analyses of LV PV and Swan‐Ganz data were performed offline using LabChart PRO software (v8.1.9, ADInstruments, Colorado Springs, CO) with the ‘PV Loop Analysis’ and ‘Cardiac Output’ modules. All load‐dependent pressure and volume indices derived from the LV catheter (i.e. maximal pressure (P max ), end‐systolic pressure (P es ), end‐diastolic pressure (P ed ), maximum rate of pressure generation (dp/dt ma x ), maximum rate of pressure decay (dp/dt min ), time constant of diastolic pressure decay (τ), end‐diastolic volume (EDV), end‐systolic volume (ESV), stroke volume (SV), ejection fraction (EF), cardiac output (Q PV ), stroke work, arterial elastance (E a )), as well as blood pressure and HR data were assessed from basal loops over a 1 min period immediately preceding the defined measurement point (i.e. prior to IVC occlusions and thermodilution). These variables were also averaged over a 1 min period within the final 3 min of the DOB stress test, prior to IVC occlusions. TPR was calculated as MAP/Q PV . PV data from IVC occlusions were analysed over 10–15 cardiac cycles for load‐independent LV function, including E es , PRSW and EDPVR, both at baseline and during the inotropic stress test with DOB. Responses to the modified Oxford challenge were analysed for beat‐by‐beat MAP, dp/dt max , EDV and R‐R interval (RRI) data, from the start time of SNP bolus until the peak MAP response to PE. Values were averaged over bins of 3 mmHg of MAP. For each individual animal, the cardio‐vagal response was assessed as the slope of RRI versus MAP, and cardio‐inotropic response was assessed as the slope of dp/dt max ‐EDV versus MAP. The operating point for each of these relationships was taken as the average value for MAP, RRI and dp/dt max ‐EDV during the resting baseline immediately prior to the SNP bolus. For each individual animal, the cardio‐vagal response was assessed as the slope of RRI versus MAP, and cardio‐inotropic response was assessed as the slope of dp/dt max ‐EDV versus MAP. The operating point for each of these relationships was taken as the average value for MAP, RRI and dp/dt max ‐EDV during the resting baseline immediately prior to the SNP bolus. Neurological assessment Hindlimb motor function was assessed throughout the study using the Porcine Thoracic Injury Behavioral Scale (PTIBS) (Lee et al., ), as described previously. Briefly, animals were clicker‐trained prior to SCI surgery for up to 1 h per day, at least five times before baseline assessment. Animals were trained to traverse a rubber runway (1.2 m wide, 5.0 m long, 4.5 mm thick 2‐ply insertion rubber, Clark Rubber, Australia) by following a target, then rewarded with a small ration of their regular food allotment. Starting 2 weeks post‐SCI and weekly thereafter, locomotor function during these assessment sessions was videotaped with three high‐definition cameras (Sony HDRCX405 HandyCam; Sony, California, USA) with the rump and hindlimbs clearly visible, and camera views were time‐synchronized with video editing software (ShotCut; MeltyTech, LLC). During each session, the animals were first placed in an ‘index position’ (i.e. with hindlimbs behind them) and then were recorded completing the task at least five times. Footage from the three cameras were used in unison to score each pass. PTIBS scores were assessed by two researchers separately, who were blinded to the animal's treatment group, and any scoring differences were resolved by consensus between researchers. Spinal cord histology Immediately following death, the spinal cord tissue was extracted (a minimum of 6 cm segment surrounding the SCI epicentre) and placed in 4% paraformaldehyde. Over the following 15 days the tissue was placed in increasing concentrations of sucrose until a 30% concentration was reached. Ensuring the injury epicentre was included in a single section, the cord tissue was cut into 1 cm sections, embedded in an optimal cutting temperature matrix (Shandon Cryomatrix, Thermo Scientific) and frozen at ‐80°C. From there, the section containing the injury epicentre was further cut into 20 µm sections and mounted onto a series of 10 slides coated with Silane Surgipath Solution (Leica), which were stored at ‐80°C. For histological analyses, sections were thawed for 2 h at room temperature, then stained with Eriochrome cyanine (EC) and counter‐stained with Neutral Red and coverslipped with Surgipath Micromount (Leica). Imaging was performed using a Zeiss Axiophot microscope (Carl Zeiss, Oberkochen, Germany) equipped with a digital camera (Axiocam 205 mono, Carl Zeiss, Oberkochen, Germany). Five images were taken at the injury epicentre, determined as the point with the lowest white matter sparing. The area of white matter tissue sparing was determined by the presence of the colour blue, and density of tissue sparing was determined by circling the blue areas by hand and subsequently dividing those by the total area of the cord. Statistical analysis and sample size calculation Data are presented as means ± standard deviation (SD). For all dependent variables, normality of distribution was assessed using the Shapiro‐Wilk test. Data derived from Swan‐Ganz (i.e. Q TD , SV TD , HR, PASP, mPAP) during SCI and haemodynamic management were assessed with a mixed‐effects model with main effects for time and treatment group. A full model fit was used with Geisser‐Greenhouse correction. Between‐group comparisons at each time point were assessed with Tukey's test, and within‐group comparisons over the course of management (i.e. versus 30 min post‐SCI) were assessed with Dunnett's test. Similarly, repeated measures from the Swan‐Ganz catheter at pre‐SCI vs . 12‐weeks post‐SCI were assessed using a mixed‐effects model with main effects for time and treatment group, and Sidak's test for multiple comparisons. For dependent measures at 12 weeks post‐SCI, effects of treatment group were assessed using Welch's ANOVA with Dunnett's T3 test for multiple comparisons in normally distributed data, and the Kruskal‐Wallis test with Dunn's test for multiple comparisons in non‐parametric data. For data in the DOB and Oxford challenges, repeated measures were assessed using a mixed‐effect model with main effects for drug (i.e. DOB, PE or SNP) and treatment group, with Sidak's test for multiple comparisons. PTIBS data were assessed using a mixed‐effects model with main effects for treatment group and time (i.e. weeks post‐SCI), and Fisher's least significant difference test for multiple comparisons versus week 2 post‐SCI. All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism (v10.1.0, GraphPad Software LLC, Boston, MA) with alpha set a priori to 0.05. All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism (v10.1.0, GraphPad Software LLC, Boston, MA) with alpha set a priori to 0.05. Prior to this study there were no published data available for load‐dependent (i.e. SV) or load‐independent (i.e. E es ) cardiac function in a porcine model of chronic T2 SCI. However, in our initial study utilizing our acute porcine model of T2 SCI (Williams et al., ) we reported data for MAP (s ρ : 9 mmHg), LV SV (s ρ : 4.1 ml) and E es (s ρ : 0.95 mmHg·ml −1 ) across four treatment groups at baseline. Based on these data, with a minimum of five animals per group and α of 0.05, we had 95% power to detect a difference of 11 mmHg in MAP, 4.1 ml in SV, 0.97 mmHg ml −1 in E es between groups. Results T2 SCI and acute haemodynamic management with DOB and norepinephrine post‐injury There were no between‐group differences in the maximum force of the impactor during the T2 contusion injury (CON: 33.93 ± 6.84 N, DOB: 28.20 ± 4.85 N, NE: 29.13 ± 4.83 N). Haemodynamic management with DOB supported acute increases in cardiac output (Q TD , Fig. ) and stroke volume (SV TD , Fig. ), which were not observed during vasopressor management with NE. Similarly, HR was augmented over the course of acute management with DOB, but unchanged in either CON or NE‐treated animals (Fig. ). There were no effects of treatment on peak systolic (pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP), Fig. ) or mean pulmonary arterial pressures (mPAP, Fig. ) over the course of acute management. Repeated measures of resting cardiopulmonary function and structure across the 12 week survival period in animals with T2 SCI Body mass increased in all groups over the 12 week recovery period ( P < 0.001 for all vs . pre‐SCI) and was not different between groups at either pre‐ or 12 weeks post‐SCI (Table ). Cardiac output assessed by thermodilution (Q TD ) was not significantly altered in any of the groups from pre‐ to 12 weeks post‐SCI, though Q TD tended to be increased in the DOB‐treated animals ( P = 0.0710). While there were no significant effects for SV TD , HR or pulmonary pressures, LVID d significantly increased in DOB‐treated animals between pre‐ and 12 weeks post‐SCI ( P = 0.0157). Resting LV function and systemic haemodynamics at 12 weeks post‐SCI Resting group‐mean averaged LV PV loops at 12 weeks post‐SCI are shown in Fig. , with additional statistics and load‐dependent haemodynamics in Fig. , Table and Table . The PV loop was relatively narrowed in the NE‐treated animals (Fig. ), reflective of a smaller stroke volume (SV PV ) in comparison to DOB‐treated animals ( P = 0.0269, Fig. ). When compared with CON, both the DOB‐ and NE‐treated groups had higher MAP ( P = 0.0147 and P = 0.00679, respectively) and SBP ( P = 0.0221 and P = 0.00210, respectively; Fig. ). The NE group had lower SV along with elevated E a ( P = 0.0258, Fig. ) and TPR ( P = 0.0345, Fig. ) when compared with CON animals. During the baseline assessments, there were no differences in E es or PRSW between the groups (Table and Table ). The NE‐treated animals, however, had a steeper EDPVR compared with CON ( P = 0.0332) and elevated E a /E es as compared with DOB‐treated animals ( P = 0.0432). Inotropic stress test with high‐dose DOB at 12 weeks post‐SCI There were no differences in load‐independent measures of LV function at baseline immediately prior to the stress test (Table and Table ). In response to 10 µg kg −1 min −1 DOB infusion, both DOB‐ and NE‐treated animals had increases to E es vs . baseline (Fig. ), and the change in E es (∆E es ) was significantly greater in the DOB‐treated group as compared with CON (9.07 ± 4.66 vs . 1.28 ± 1.41 mmHg ml −1 , P = 0.0163). However, only the DOB‐treated animals had improvements to PRSW ( P = 0.0227 vs . BSL) and Q PV ( P = 0.0491) during the stress test. Operating points for both relationships were not different between treatment groups. While the average cardio‐inotropic slope was notably shallow in CON (Fig. ), both DOB‐ and NE‐treated groups displayed inotropic responsiveness to changes in MAP,

Inotropic and chronotropic responses to blood pressure challenge during modified Oxford test The cardio‐inotropic and cardio‐vagal responses to the modified Oxford challenge are illustrated in Fig. . Operating points for both relationships were not different between treatment groups. While the average cardio‐inotropic slope was notably shallow in CON (Fig. ), both DOB‐ and NE‐treated groups displayed inotropic responsiveness to changes in MAP, and the cardio‐inotropic slope was significantly greater in magnitude in the DOB‐treated group when compared with CON ( P = 0.0251). There were no differences in these slopes for CON vs . NE ( P = 0.751) or DOB vs . NE ( P = 0.597). Similarly, there were no significant differences in the cardio‐vagal relationships between any groups (CON vs . DOB: P = 0.925; CON vs . NE: P = 0.624) (Fig. ). The peak responses to SNP and PE boluses are provided in Table and Table . There were no group × drug interactions detected for any of the outlined dependent variables; however, the NE‐treated animals were the only group with significant reductions to Q during the phenylephrine infusion, due to a reduction in HR rather than SV. Histological analyses of the spinal cord at 12 weeks post‐SCI Histological analyses using EC staining were performed to quantify white matter sparing. At the injury epicentre, DOB‐treated animals had significantly higher EC density than NE animals ( P = 0.0411; Fig. ). However, there were no differences between CON vs . NE ( P = 0.989) or DOB ( P = 0.142). Assessments of hindlimb motor function via PTIBS from 2 weeks to 12 weeks post‐injury in animals with T2 SCI From weekly assessments of hindlimb motor function with PTIBS, there was an overall effect of time (Fig. ). However, there were no significant within‐group effects over the 12 week recovery period, nor between‐group differences in PTIBS scores at any time point. See Table in the Appendix for P values of mixed‐effects model and pairwise comparisons. Discussion The findings from this study provide further insight to the potential benefits of clinical management strategies that target the heart following acute high‐level SCI. Chronically surviving pigs with T2 SCI to 12 weeks post‐injury underscores the overall haemodynamic benefits of both DOB and NE‐based acute haemodynamic management, while further uncovering important disparities in cardiovascular outcomes related to those approaches. Notably, the acute data confirm that cardio‐centric management with DOB supports MAP through enhanced SV and Q, whereas NE directly targets the vasculature. Following 12 weeks’ survival, while both DOB and NE‐based management were associated with improved resting blood pressure, DOB animals exhibited more white matter sparing than NE‐treated animals, implying improved neuroprotection. Cardiovascular responses to DOB <italic toggle="yes">versus</italic> vasopressor management Consistent with our previous acute T2 SCI study (Williams et al., ), we measured the haemodynamic responses during the acute treatment period and found that DOB‐based management was associated with augmented LV SV and Q. In contrast to the DOB‐treated animals, NE‐based management did not acutely elevate LV output, likely due to the concurrent increase in afterload (i.e. arterial elastance). To our knowledge, only three other studies have explored the use of DOB in the acute setting of SCI, two of which combined DOB with vasopressors (Bilello et al., ; Lehmann et al., ). Levi and colleagues (Levi et al., ) combined fluid replacement and inotropic support with either dopamine or DOB (mean doses 5–6 µg kg −1 min −1 ) in patients with acute cervical SCI. They reported patients receiving inotropic treatment had improved cardiac index, HR and systemic vascular resistance index. Furthermore, non‐surviving patients had significantly lower cardiac index than survivors. While Levi et al. did not stratify these outcomes based on DOB vs . dopamine treatment, their findings highlight the benefits of targeting the heart and maintaining cardiac output for adequate tissue and spinal cord oxygen delivery in the acute setting of high‐level SCI. The potential cardiovascular benefits associated with acute haemodynamic management are further highlighted by the data at 12 weeks post‐SCI. Both the DOB and NE cohorts had improved MAP and SBP compared with untreated controls, reinforcing the long‐term benefits of haemodynamic management compared with no management at all. However, the haemodynamics underpinning the elevated blood pressure differed between the treatment groups: SV was significantly larger in the DOB‐treated group vs . NE‐treated group, whereas TPR and Ea was markedly higher in the NE cohort vs . CON, suggesting a relatively greater cardiac versus vascular support of resting blood pressure in the DOB‐ versus NE‐treated animals, respectively. Indeed, cardiac output and SV appeared to be restricted by the higher LV afterload in the NE‐treated animals, as indicated by elevated E a . Moreover, the slope of the EDPVR in NE‐treated animals was significantly elevated vs . CON, suggesting marked LV stiffening. We suspect that the LV stiffening in the NE cohort may be linked to a prolonged increase in afterload associated with arterial stiffening; however, it is unclear how NE‐based haemodynamic management might specifically contribute to long‐term cardiovascular stiffening in high‐level SCI. While there were no significant differences in resting load‐independent systolic function, the LV responses to dynamic challenges did vary amongst the groups. During the DOB stress test, E es was not significantly altered in CON but did respond in both the DOB and NE‐treated animals, indicating some preservation of BAR‐mediated contractile reserve. In our prior study on acute T2 SCI (Williams et al., ), the contractile response to an identical DOB stress test was blunted by ∼33% in untreated controls at 4 h post‐SCI. Untreated rodents with chronic T3 SCI have similarly exhibited blunted SV and Q responses to DOB stress tests (DeVeau et al., ). In the current study we further observed that DOB‐treated animals had enhanced responses of PRSW and Q during the DOB stress test vs . CON, which were not observed in the NE‐treated group. Such differences in systolic responsiveness may result from differences in ventricular–vascular coupling, as seen with the elevated E a /E es in NE vs . DOB‐treated animals. The LV responses during the modified Oxford test also varied, with stronger contractile responses in the DOB‐treated animals. Indeed, the slope of the LV contractile response, assessed as dp/dt max ‐EDV (Blaudszun et al., )) versus MAP, was significantly higher in the DOB‐treated animals vs . CON, implying they were able to mount greater contractile responses during reductions in blood pressure. The variability in this slope was much greater in the NE group and ultimately not statistically different from CON or DOB. The cardio‐vagal response to the Oxford test was otherwise comparable between the groups, which was generally expected given the vagus nerve travels outside the spinal cord (Gondim et al., ; Mathias & Frankel, ) and thus not directly impacted by the trauma of SCI. While impairments to the arterial baroreflex have been identified in the context of high‐level SCI (Draghici & Taylor, ; Phillips et al., ), this may be the first study to assess shifts in the cardio‐inotropic responses to a baroreflex challenge in a chronic model of SCI. Potential mechanisms related to acute haemodynamic management With EC staining assessments of the spinal cord, we found that DOB‐treated animals exhibited significantly greater white matter sparing vs . NE‐treated animals. This finding nicely compliments our previous study with the acute porcine model of T2 SCI (Williams et al., ), in which we demonstrated that acute DOB treatment improved spinal cord oxygenation and reduced haemorrhage within the initial 4 h post‐SCI, whereas NE treatment exacerbated intraparenchymal haemorrhage. The haemorrhagic implications of NE are supported by multiple studies using animal models of SCI (Osterholm & Mathews, ; Rawe et al., ; Soubeyrand et al., ), and likely result from α 1 ‐receptor‐mediated vasoconstriction in the intact spinal cord vessels (Noris et al., ; Ruffolo, ). We have hypothesized that DOB‐based treatment provides a more favourable series of mechanisms, whereby both β 2 ‐adrenergic receptor stimulation alongside improved shear‐mediated vasodilatation may ultimately optimize microvascular flow in the injured spinal cord and mitigate haemorrhage as compared with NE‐based treatments (Williams et al., ). As such, we believe that acute treatment with DOB may reduce secondary injury via improved blood flow and oxygenation. This, in turn, could protect descending sympathetic pathways to the cardiac projecting sympathetic preganglionic neurons in the T2–T5 region of the spinal cord and ultimately preserve the sympathetic support of cardiac function following high‐level SCI. The temporal nature of secondary injury is crucial when considering treatment for acute traumatic SCI. In this study, we were able to demonstrate that even a 6 h treatment duration was associated with profound shifts in chronic cardiovascular function. The temporal nature of secondary injury is crucial when considering treatment for acute traumatic SCI. In this study, we were able to demonstrate that even a 6 h treatment duration was associated with profound shifts in chronic cardiovascular function. While seemingly short, the immediacy of treatment administration at 30 min post‐SCI likely drove their significant long‐term impacts. Local ischaemia is a major component of the secondary injury cascade, which, combined with inflammation, excitotoxicity and oedema, ultimately promotes necrosis of the injured cord tissue (Hejrati et al., ; Tator & Fehlings, ), emphasizing the need to mitigate tissue hypoxia and haemorrhagic necrosis as quickly as possible for improved outcomes (Ryken et al., ). Early studies have further shown haemorrhage and erythrocyte extravasation in the perivascular space as early as 15 min, with destruction of the myelin sheaths at 4 h post‐SCI (Dohrmann et al., ). We have previously shown that even 4 h of DOB or NE management can alter spinal cord tissue flow, oxygenation and haemorrhaging (Williams et al., ), highlighting the temporal importance of these strategies. This theme is further highlighted by clinical studies linking early MAP support (Hawryluk et al., ) and surgical intervention (i.e. within 24 h) to superior neurological recovery in patients with cervical SCI (Badhiwala et al., ; Ghajarzadeh & Saberi, ; Jug et al., ). Therefore, it is reasonable that interventions like the 6 h haemodynamic management in the current study can influence long‐term outcomes when applied early following SCI. Considerations The assessment of neurological function with PTIBS was previously established and validated by our group in a T10 model of SCI (Kim et al., ; Lee et al., ). In the current study, the PTIBS scale may have lacked sensitivity to adequately characterize neurological recovery in the T2 injury model. This was the first time this T2 model survived beyond the acute injury day, and the loss of both hindlimb and forelimb function, in addition to altered trunk control, was greater than anticipated. On the PTIBS scale we saw minimal recovery from on average 1.5 to 2 over the 12 weeks of study, whereas previous low‐thoracic injury studies with similar SCI characteristics (i.e. 50 g weight dropped 20 cm) have seen improved PTIBS scores from 4 to 7 over 12 weeks’ recovery (Lee et al., ). We were unable to appropriately assess any improvements in forelimb function due to a lack of validated scales; thus, the development of such tools to assess righting and forelimb function would be highly valuable for a more in‐depth and injury‐specific assessment of neurological function in future studies utilizing similar models of high‐level SCI. The clinical application of DOB for haemodynamic management has been overlooked, with some concerns of potential vasodilatation and reflex bradycardia (Ball, ; Ploumis et al., ). While DOB does have moderate β 2 ‐agonist effects, we have observed in the current and previous study (Williams et al., ) that DOB elevates MAP to a similar degree seen with NE due to its inotropic effects on the heart. Moreover, DOB can further improve spinal cord oxygenation acutely post‐SCI (Williams et al., ) and other studies have shown that its vasodilatory effects may even reduce haemorrhagic necrosis by improving local dilatation of the spinal cord microvasculature (Rawe et al., ). Consideration should be given to the relatively small sample size of the present study. Conducting large‐animal studies such as this is time‐consuming, expensive and needs to judiciously balance the need for a sufficient ‘ n ’ against the ethical considerations of animal research. Unfortunately, as is the nature of this type of research, we were not able to assess all outcomes on all animals. We have been careful to report exact sample sizes in the tables for each comparison and have additionally provided all pairwise comparisons as appended tables to this manuscript. Unfortunately, the limited sample size for some outcomes meant we were underpowered for some of our outcomes and this undoubtedly has limited the interpretation of some of our data. Conclusions Haemodynamic management with NE is the cornerstone of the acute critical care management of individuals with SCI. We have shown that DOB is as efficacious as NE for maintaining blood pressure during the acute post‐injury period, but enables superior neuroprotection compared with NE. Moreover, when viewing the collective evidence across all of our chronic outcomes, we believe that DOB produces a more favourable haemodynamic profile compared with control animals as indicated by better resting and dynamic heart function. In contrast, haemodynamic management with NE appears to come at the cost of increased peripheral resistance and ventricular stiffening as
